newsitem.title: ITALY: Marzotto to gain most as merger fails.
newsitem.headline: Marzotto to gain most as merger fails.

text.p: Italy's Marzotto is best placed to gain from its failed merger after the family-controlled company pulled out of a deal mastermined by Mediobanca that would have ended family control, analysts said on Monday.

The shock decision on Saturday by Marzotto to walk away from a merger that appeared sealed two months ago pushed all shares involved lower, but analysts said Marzotto would be the main gainer and should continue now to focus on textiles.

In early March, merchant bank Mediobanca brokered a plan to merger Marzotto with Holding Partecipazioni Industriali (HPI) to form one of the world's largest textile groups, but one that would also have had some one-third of its sales in publishing.

"It looks good news for Marzotto and bad news for HPI," said one analyst in Milan, adding that the Marzotto family had decided against diluting its control and effectively abdicating power to deal-maker Mediobanca and its close ally Fiat.

He said that the Marzotto family would have lost control, and created a group where Fiat could have offloaded its chemicals and fibre company Snia BPD, leaving a merged group to go off on a buying spree with its cash pile.
Marzotto shares were off 1.92 percent at 12,170 lire, HPI down 6.26 percent at 870 lire and Mediobanca down 3.68 percent at 10,235 lire in an otherwise steady Milan bourse.

The merger was to create a group with 8.24 trillion lire ($4.8 billion) of annual sales, linking Marzotto's textile business and its majority stake in Hugo Boss with HPI's clothing interests -- the Fila sportswear business and GFT, which produces clothes for top designers such as Armani and Prada.
HPI's publishing offshoot Rizzoli Corriere della Sera would also have been folded into the new group under the merger plan.

The stock market had initially greeted the merger news positively, but since then Marzotto shares have underperformed the market as some questioned the limited synergies of the merger and the logic of linking textiles and publishing.

The newly merged group to have been called Gruppo Industriale Marzotto or "big GIM" would have had the head of the Marzotto family Pietro Marzotto as chairman and Fiat chairman Cesare Romiti's son Maurizio as managing director. Fiat would have had the biggest shareholding at 17.3 percent, the Marzotto family 12.4 percent and Mediobanca 10.5 percent.
Once more it cast a spotlight on Mediobanca with a second major failure in two years after its SuperGemina deal to link Gemina with the Ferruzzi Finanziaria empire was abandoned.
Mediobanca spun off the industrial interests of Gemina into HPI and tried again last year only to end in failure again.

"Overall the most negative aspect is on the way deals are done in Italy," said head of equities trading Marco Nascembini at Merrill Lynch. Other analysts said deals should be more transparent and show more regard for minority shareholders.

But for Marzotto alone, the outlook is still encouraging with the group expected to remain clearly focused and set for good results. Analyst Elena Sottanella at brokers Pasfin said she expects group net profits of 70 billion lire in 1997, up from 57.7 billion lire in 1996.

"I think what is happening to the share price is a normal reaction and we believe the share price will fall in the short term, but this is not justified by the share price multiple of the shares and its prospects," she said.
For HPI, the uncertainty will remain about who it may link up with, what the group does with its cash and the future within the group for Italy's second largest publisher RCS. ($1=1,710 lire)
